rv.q: There is nothing whatsoever joyous about this chilly, fractured take on “Othello,” a conception that has a dystopian sensibility running through its core.
In Roston’s expert hands, Othello is thrown, not moved yet to suspicion and anger.
It is compact, judiciously and smartly edited, and fits admirably into the hands of co-directors Charles Newell and Gabrielle Randle-Bent in a challenging and engaging 100 minutes or so.
Let’s Play Highly Recommends, The Tragedy of Othello, the Moor of Venice at Court Theater.
The production powerfully captures both the timeless and timely elements it aims for.
The Tragedy of Othello, the Moor of Venice is a dynamically engaging, crisply edited, jarring production.

Others, myself included, may admire the risk-taking production that challenges our previous exposure to The Moor of Venice, but still leave the Court feeling the interpretation cost the play more than it offered in fresh insights.

This perpetual conundrum is neatly sketched in a Court Theatre production of "Othello" that otherwise leaves too much on the cutting room floor and, in its overwrought stylized mannerisms, loses sight of a thousand nuances, then simply throws away the drama's tragic consummation.
Whether you’ve seen it a dozen times or have never dipped a toe into Shakespeare’s work, this is the way to experience Othello .

cn.t: Court Theatre's streamlined 100-minute "Othello" earns mixed reviews for its intimate, compact staging and strong performances, particularly Roston's thoughtful lead, though some find the chilly, fractured approach lacking in emotional power.
